title: Strengthen Firm and Client Relationships With Shared Spaces
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Shared infrastructure: Harvey proposes continuous client collaboration

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Harvey accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and concretely extends it through shared workflows, client-generated drafts subject to lawyer review, reusable playbooks, permissions and audit trails. It illustrates operating-model redesign across several legal workflows, although its productivity and outcome claims remain vendor assertions without comparative or quantitative validation.
qs: Law firms can also share purpose-built Workflows and Playbooks to deliver automation without losing human judgment or insight.
Workflows enable clients to generate first drafts for your review, cutting down on back and forth.

st.t: Shared infrastructure: Harvey proposes continuous client collaboration
st.an: Harvey directly advances the cluster’s proposition that shared, permissioned AI infrastructure can replace fragmented handoffs with continuous firm–client collaboration and self-service. It also preserves lawyer review in key workflows and describes access controls, while offering product claims and illustrative use cases rather than measured evidence of transformation or budget effects.
qs: Workflows enable clients to generate first drafts for your review, cutting down on back and forth.

Legal and compliance professionals can leverage shared Spaces to share proposed compliance program enhancements for outside counsel to review and comment — turning gap analysis into an ongoing dialogue rather than a periodic exercise.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s application-layer thesis by presenting Shared Spaces as embedded, cross-organisational legal infrastructure combining firm knowledge, workflows, client collaboration and granular controls. It also aligns with the cluster’s qualifications: lawyers retain review responsibility, some functionality is prospective, and claimed efficiency or relationship benefits are vendor assertions rather than measured outcomes. It does not establish durable defensibility.
qs: Share Vaults to give clients a secure place to work alongside your teams on key documents — or to self-serve answers drawn directly from your firm’s knowledge and expertise.
Law firms can also share purpose-built Workflows and Playbooks to deliver automation without losing human judgment or insight.

kp.k: Shared workspaces extend collaboration beyond firm boundaries
kp.d: Harvey presents shared Spaces as enabling law firms, clients and cross-functional teams to collaborate within its AI platform. The December 4, 2025 announcement describes shared Spaces as available now but guest-account support as forthcoming, distinguishing current collaboration capabilities from planned access for clients who are not Harvey customers.
qs: Harvey makes this possible now with shared Spaces.
Shared Spaces will also support guest accounts, enabling firms to collaborate with clients who aren't Harvey customers yet.

kp.k: Clients self-serve firm knowledge while lawyers review drafts
kp.d: Harvey describes a division of work in which clients use shared Vaults to obtain answers from firm knowledge and run firm-built Workflows to produce first drafts for lawyer review. Playbooks turn firm positions and market intelligence into repeatable negotiation guidance. The source frames this as automation retaining human judgment, rather than independent replacement of legal review.
qs: Share Vaults to give clients a secure place to work alongside your teams on key documents — or to self-serve answers drawn directly from your firm’s knowledge and expertise.
Law firms can also share purpose-built Workflows and Playbooks to deliver automation without losing human judgment or insight.
Workflows enable clients to generate first drafts for your review, cutting down on back and forth.
Playbooks package market intelligence and firm positions into repeatable guidance, helping drive stronger outcomes in negotiations.

kp.k: Permissions and audit trails govern cross-organization knowledge sharing
kp.d: Harvey says collaboration can require administrator approval and use object-level permissions and audit trails to protect proprietary knowledge. It asserts that legal teams control what they share and that Harvey does not access, view or share their artifacts or tools. These are the vendor's stated confidentiality and control provisions.
qs: Cross-organization collaboration can be configured to require admin approval, with granular, object-level permissions (e.g., view, comment, run, edit) to protect proprietary knowledge while keeping work moving.
Audit trails provide transparency and accountability.
The prompts you input, documents you upload, work product you generate, and Workflows you build remain private to the legal teams that create them.
Harvey does not access, view, or share your artifacts or tools.

kp.k: Transactional workflows combine client execution with joint legal analysis
kp.d: For M&A, Harvey proposes client-run diligence workflows, simultaneous analysis of target documents, and Playbook-generated redlines or edited drafts subject to firm review. Shared closing workspaces support monitoring, decisions and issue resolution. Faster execution and strategic alignment are presented as expected benefits of this workflow, not as measured transaction outcomes.
qs: Clients can run due diligence workflows independently, reducing initial wait time.

When target documents arrive, analyze them simultaneously in shared Vaults where Harvey surfaces risks and extracts terms across thousands of files, enabling both teams to identify issues and make decisions together as patterns emerge.
Embed negotiation strategy with Playbooks that clients can apply to agreements to propose redlines or generate edited drafts for your review, streamlining each negotiation cycle.
Throughout closing, track progress in the same workspace, where both sides can monitor review status, capture decisions, and resolve issues in real time.

kp.k: Litigation collaboration combines legal arguments with client business context
kp.d: Harvey describes AI-assisted discovery analysis, jointly constructed chronologies and evidence tables, collaborative pleading preparation, and workflows using case law and connected sources to support strategy. Clients contribute business context and facts while firms develop legal arguments and questions. Reduced analysis delays and faster strategic decisions are vendor claims rather than reported study findings.
qs: Review discovery and client documents simultaneously in shared Vaults where Harvey helps lawyers identify patterns, extract key facts, and flag potential inconsistencies across large discovery sets.
Teams create shared chronologies and evidence tables together — minimizing multi-day delays for analysis.
Draft pleadings collaboratively as firms develop legal arguments while clients provide business context through shared Artifacts.
Share Workflows that analyze applicable case law, precedent, and other connected sources to generate case strategy and help clients make faster decisions on which motions to pursue.
Prepare for trial as a unified team using shared transcripts, case notes, and exhibits where clients identify key business facts while firms craft legal questions.

kp.k: Compliance shifts toward continuous client–outside counsel dialogue
kp.d: Harvey proposes that in-house legal and compliance teams run firm-built workflows comparing compliance programs against evolving regulations, then share proposed improvements for outside counsel review. It also describes real-time collaboration on breach materiality and mitigation. The claimed change is from periodic gap analysis to ongoing interaction; greater analytical depth without larger budgets is asserted as a benefit.
qs: Create a continuous intelligence loop where clients run firm-built Workflows to benchmark compliance program elements (including policies, training, and risk assessment) against evolving regulations.

Legal and compliance professionals can leverage shared Spaces to share proposed compliance program enhancements for outside counsel to review and comment — turning gap analysis into an ongoing dialogue rather than a periodic exercise.
If breaches are identified, collaborate in real time to assess materiality and mitigation strategies, making precedents and response frameworks available quickly through Harvey.
Firms deliver proactive, timely value while in-house teams gain analytical depth without expanding budgets.

kp.k: Governance workspaces address directors' fragmented access to information
kp.d: Harvey identifies dispersed corporate records and independent directors' limited involvement in daily operations as obstacles to oversight. It presents shared Spaces as tools through which governance teams can give directors access to necessary information, without reporting measured oversight improvements.
qs: Independent directors, in particular, are less involved with the day-to-day operations of the entities they oversee and face challenges where information necessary for their critical oversight role sits across thousands of documents.
Shared Spaces empower Corporate Governance teams to equip directors with the information and tools necessary to perform their critical oversight role.

kp.k: Firm-branded AI access creates recurring client engagement
kp.d: Harvey argues that shared Spaces can position firms as guides to clients' AI adoption, with branded spaces creating repeat interactions beyond individual work-product exchanges. It links this model to differentiation and deeper relationships while preserving firm control over expertise; these are vendor claims about client-service strategy.
qs: This positions firms as the driver of their clients' AI journey while creating ongoing engagement.
Clients can return to the firm's branded Space for quick insights and answers, strengthening relationships and creating new touchpoints.
Firms deliver more proactive value while maintaining strong, admin-configurable control over their expertise.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that shared AI workspaces accelerate legal delivery, enable client self-service with lawyer review, and strengthen firm–client relationships.
pts.d: The Harvey Team attributes these changes to shared Spaces, Vaults, Workflows, Playbooks and Artifacts. Clients can obtain answers from firm knowledge and generate first drafts, while firms retain review and judgment. Sharing work products and repeatable firm guidance is said to reduce back-and-forth, speed review and improve negotiation outcomes. Branded workspaces and repeat visits are also presented as sources of firm differentiation and continuing client engagement. The claimed model combines client self-service with lawyer augmentation, rather than asserting wholesale replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that shared AI tools accelerate transaction execution and litigation analysis while improving joint decision-making.
pts.d: For M&A, the source describes clients independently generating diligence requests and drafts, joint analysis across thousands of target files, application of firm negotiation guidance and shared closing-status tracking. It claims these functions reduce waiting and negotiation cycles and enable earlier decisions. For litigation, it describes joint discovery analysis, chronologies, evidence tables, pleading development, AI-assisted case strategy and shared trial materials. These are presented as ways to reduce analysis delays and align clients and lawyers on evidence and strategy, not as reported results from identified matters.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that AI collaboration supports continuous compliance work, better-informed corporate oversight and greater client analytical depth without larger budgets.
pts.d: The compliance scenario replaces periodic gap analysis with ongoing comparison of program elements against regulations and dialogue with outside counsel. It also proposes real-time collaboration on breaches, materiality and mitigation. Here, benchmarking means comparing compliance programs against regulatory requirements, not measuring AI model performance. For governance, shared Spaces are said to help teams provide directors, particularly independent directors, with information dispersed across corporate records. Budget-neutral gains in analytical depth are asserted for in-house teams and clients.

pts.k: The Harvey Team claims that cross-organization AI collaboration can preserve confidentiality and firm control over proprietary knowledge.
pts.d: The source presents configurable administrator approval, object-level permissions, audit trails and creator-controlled sharing as the mechanisms enabling collaboration without surrendering confidentiality or process control. It also states that Harvey does not access, view or share users’ artifacts or tools. These are the vendor’s security and privacy assertions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is a first-party product description and illustrative practice scenarios, not reported empirical evaluation.
pts.d: The article is attributed to the Harvey Team and explains how named product capabilities are expected to produce the claimed benefits. Its M&A, litigation, compliance and governance sections offer prospective workflows rather than identified client cases. It provides no cited studies, model benchmarks, measured time or cost comparisons, customer outcome data or independent security assessment. Statements about analysis in minutes, thousands of files, reduced multi-day delays and unchanged budgets are assertions without accompanying measurement methods or results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Core capabilities are presented as available on December 4, 2025; guest accounts are described as forthcoming without a release date.
pts.d: The article says shared Spaces make collaboration possible “now,” and generally frames benefits as available through adoption of the described workflows. It separately says guest accounts “will” be supported, despite its opening description including noncustomers among potential collaborators. No quantified adoption horizon is supplied. Benefits depend on firms sharing relevant documents, expertise, Workflows and Playbooks, clients participating and permissions allowing access. Draft-generation examples explicitly retain firm review, while administrator approval is configurable rather than universally required. Timing claims such as analysis in minutes are task-level assertions, not longitudinal evidence.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed beneficiaries are law firms, corporate clients, in-house legal and compliance teams, deal and litigation teams, cross-functional partners and directors.
pts.d: Provider-side law firms are portrayed as delivering faster, more proactive services, differentiating their offerings and maintaining control of expertise while deepening client engagement. Buyer-side clients gain self-service, visibility, quicker decisions and analytical depth without budget growth. Transaction and litigation participants gain shared analysis and coordination; in-house legal and compliance professionals gain ongoing regulatory dialogue with outside counsel; governance teams and independent directors gain access to dispersed oversight information. Future guest access extends participation to clients without Harvey subscriptions. No firm-size-specific impacts, staffing reductions or access-to-justice outcomes are claimed.
